title: Even with AI, multiplayer is NOT a walk in the park
author: SuperCamouflageShark
selftext:
Fellow/future AI devs, take this story as a word of caution.

When I started using Rosebud to make my first person horror maze game, I was against multiplayer. I knew it would be difficult and I didn't think the game needed it. But my curiosity piqued when i saw someone else's game seemed to handle multiplayer flawlessly.

So I looked into it, decided on Co-Op with 3 players Max in a lobby, and before you know it, I had set up peer to peer with lobby codes. Created a simple little lobby, an Alias textbox to show who's who, got my friend to playtest. When he moved, i saw him move on my end, and vice versa. Yay! It works!

Then the gameplay *actually* started.

There's a section in each run where you collect keys to bring to a statue to unlock the exit. There was a bunch of "Did you pick up a key?" "Yeah, did you?" "No, i still see all four keys".

When i got killed, my friend was supposed to revive me. While there's a minimap, and the maze isn't huge, i had no way of showing WHERE i was for him to revive me. When he finally did, my spectating overlay disappeared.

Then 15 seconds after reviving, the game ended for everyone, displaying game over. Why? Because there was no logic to let the game continue after that revival.

By the end of the session, my notepad next to me was *filled* with things i needed to fix, simply because i let AI handle the connecting, the p2p, and simple gameplay elements like reviving.

My point to this: *you need to think of EVERYTHING that can and may happen in multiplayer.* You cannot pretend AI will take care of it and it'll just be "duplicating singleplayer for multiple people" like I had initially thought. *No*. That's how you end up saying "That's not supposed to happen" every 5 minutes during testing.

Don't be like me. If you have multiplayer, think ahead about your game mechanics. What happens to the other players once this person does \_\_\_? What do they see? Does *everyone* know that objective has been accomplished? Is there any audio letting others know that this happened? Text?

Thanks for reading🤘

replies.author: Spudly42
replies.body:
Once you have the mindset, it's not so bad to think of the scenarios that should sync and how that should work.  You start to really think about how to make things more deterministic to reduce how much you need to explicitly sync.

But the testing, the testing to me is the main thing that scales with multiplayer.  You may spend 10-20% more time on the code, but testing takes 50% more time and you need a good way to handle multiple clients.

comments.author: uxarya
comments.body:
Hey, I’m a product designer who likes to play games occasionally. I had an interaction idea for a football game which I decided to build with the help of AI. Once I had the basics in place and the game felt playable. I decided to to add 1v1 gameplay. Codex used partykit to implement it, while testing out the implementation the gameplay felt very laggy and unplayable in a 1v1 setup. With some more prompting it felt better. Next, I decided to take it for a spin with a friend. It refused to connect with another player over a different wifi. With some more prompting it added some debugging message with the help of which it fixed the connection issue, but the gameplay was laggy again. After some research I asked it to leverage WebRTC for the 1v1 gameplay implementation. After this it started working flawlessly (as of now).

Here’s what I built: https://scrollfc.vercel.app/ (please check it out on a laptop)

It was tough and I had almost dropped the 1v1 gameplay idea. It was a learning experience for sure.

comments.author: hobobum
comments.body:
This is basic development: you need to create user stories and acceptance criteria, feed it to the AI, and then QA from there (for best results). You will inevitably miss some interactions, but what you’re describing is entirely predictable if you just vibe prompts and expect them to work. Not saying this condescendingly, just trying to share some best practices (15 years professional game dev at some very well known studios).

You can also look up or ask you LLM common boilerplate requirements and considerations or edge cases for multi-player. Think logically through LITERALLY every moment and action from when a user boots up the game through when their session ends. What do they click? What are the key beats within the player experience? Within each beat, what is an action they will take or “thing” that will happen? How don you want it to work? Where are there unknowns? Literally map that out and consider all interactions and requirements you have for how each should function. Anyways, good luck!

comments.author: DoggoCentipede
comments.body:
I feel like people need to get off AI game dev and *start* in just gamedev because all of this is really basic gamedev stuff. 

AI isn't magic. If you don't tell it exactly what you want it's going to fill in the gaps with who knows what.  Often just the shortest path from A->B that meets the *letter* of your request, not the spirit.

So all of these one shot prompt or vague "build me this!" results might seem wonderful on first glance, but they're thin veneers. At best they are vertical slices, but they fall over under the slightest deviation from the script.

You still have to do work. You still have to know how things work to make an experience that isn't super flat or super buggy.

replies.author: DoggoCentipede
replies.body:
One key thing to remember is adding multiplayer after the fact is almost impossible without planning ahead.

One strategy is to write the single player as multiplayer locally always so you run a server process along side the client. Then at least you are architectured for it even if it is only zero latency that you've tested at. 

This can also make it easier to playtest split screen modes or just having a second client open because it's no different from someone else joining.

replies.author: Time_Cat_5212
replies.body: It's helpful to do a brainstorming process before specifying anything.  Like what are my options for multiplayer?  How do they do it in (example)?  What are pros and cons?

replies.author: DoggoCentipede
replies.body:
Yes absolutely. Brainstorm have it write down each feature/technology discussion into per-topic files. Record what was investigated, what fit the design goals, what didn't, what you chose and why. Also criteria for revisiting the decision later if dependent variables change.

You need to be deliberate with decisions and know the implications and constraints.

And scope tightly. If you have lots of ideas, make it clear that some are just things to write down to explore later or in another project. Don't let it become a do-everything project that never functions. Start small. Build independent prototypes of individual systems.  Do it in one project but make each one have a way to run the system stand alone, full test suite on functionality (not design values, you have to keep tests from breaking any time you adjust a value) that runs after every build.

Tell it to make scripts to do create a build, run the tests. Don't expect it to remember to do it all. It will decide not to do stuff. The only way you can make sure something happens consistently is remove the agent from that part of the loop and make it machinery of the process.

comments.author: lazy_lockstep
comments.body:
Yeah, this is a game design problem, rather than strictly a coding problem, so it does fall to the human to specify.  

To make conceptualizing the problem simpler, I would consider a few different classes of entity:  
Player  
AllPlayers  
Team (for groupings in competitive games)  
Party (for groupings in cooperative games)

Then it's the game designer's call how the behavior should work.

a. If (player) reaches exit -> move player to next area  
vs  
b. If (player) reaches exit -> party.players to the next area  
vs  
c. If (party.players) in exit trigger -> party.players moves to next area, else "you must gather your party, before venturing forth"
